Surah 105: The Elephant

It is Meccan, and its verses number five, with no disagreement about either. It seems that when it included the mocking and slandering by the disbelievers, which was a kind of plotting against him (peace be upon him), it followed that with the story of the People of the Elephant, to indicate that the outcome of their plotting in this world is their destruction. For the care of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for His Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) is stronger and more complete than His care for the House. So the surah points to their end in this world right after explaining their end in the Hereafter. It is also possible that it serves as evidence for what was alluded to earlier, that wealth will not avail them anything against Allah, the Exalted, or as evidence of His power, Mighty and Majestic, to carry out what He threatened those disbelievers with in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing Fire﴾, and so on.

[Page 234 continues below]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the People of the Elephant?﴾

The apparent meaning is that the address is to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him). The interrogative hamza (alif) is for affirming his seeing, by denying its absence. The seeing is visual, but it is used figuratively for knowledge, either as a verbal metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) or as a metonymy (majaz mursal), since it is a cause of knowledge. It is also possible to take it as knowledge from the beginning, but that is more eloquent. His knowledge of this (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) came from his having heard it through multiple reliable transmissions (mutawatir).

The word "how" (kayfa) is in the accusative position as a verbal noun (masdar) governed by "dealt" (fa'ala), meaning: what kind of dealing He dealt. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject, and the manner is the actual object of the seeing in "Have you not seen," because of the interrogative sense. The clause serves in place of the two objects of "saw" (tara). Some have permitted making "how" the object of "saw," since the interrogative sense has been detached from it, as in the commentary on the Sharh al-Miftah al-Sharifi.

Abu Hayyan explicitly ruled this out, because it observes its need to begin the sentence, preserving the ruling of its original form. Also, the seeing is linked to the manner of Allah's action, not to the thing itself, so that it would not be said, "Have you not seen what your Lord did..." This is to magnify the event and to announce that it occurred in an awe-inspiring manner and an astonishing form, indicating the immense power of Allah, the completeness of His knowledge and wisdom, its strangeness, and the nobility of His Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him). For this, as many have said, is among the preliminary signs (irhas, signs preceding prophethood) for what has been narrated: that the event occurred in the year in which the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) was born.

Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir, the teacher of al-Bukhari, said: No scholar doubts this, and there is consensus on it. Whatever contradicts it is an error. That is, [the error is the view] that it occurred ten years before, or fifteen years before, or twenty-three years before, or thirty years before, or forty years before, or seventy years before, which are the views mentioned in the books of biography (siyar). According to the first view, which is the preferred one that the majority hold, it has been said that his birth (peace be upon him) was on the day that Allah sent the birds against the People of the Elephant in that same year. This is mentioned in the History of Ibn Hibban, and it is the apparent meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas: "He (peace be upon him) was born on the day of the Elephant." Al-Suhayli held that he (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) was born fifty days after it, and it occurred in Muharram, while the birth was in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal. The memorizer al-Dimyati said: fifty-five days after it. It has been said: forty days, and it has been said: one month. The well-known view is the one al-Suhayli held.

In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿your Lord﴾, there is a kind of allusion to the preliminary sign. That this was for the nobility of the House and the supplication of the Friend (Khalil, Abraham, peace be upon him) does not contradict it being a preliminary sign. Likewise, it does not contradict it that the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) said at Hudaybiyyah, when his she-camel knelt and the people said, "She has balked," that is, she became stubborn: "She has not balked, but the one who withholds the Elephant has withheld her."

For he did not claim that this was only for the preliminary sign. Such causes do not harm by being multiple. The story of the Qaramita and others supports the preliminary sign.

The detailed account of the story is that Abraha al-Ashram ibn al-Sabah al-Habashi, as Ibn Ishaq and others said, the one known by the kunya Abu Yaksum with the letter sin (unpointed, s), is not contradicted by the name Abraha, based on the claim that its meaning in Abyssinian is "white-faced," as is not hidden.

It has been said that he was from Himyar. He rebelled against Arbat, the king of Yemen, who was before Ashamah al-Najashi (with a kasra on the nun), two years into his reign. They fought each other, and al-Ashram had posted his slave Atarah behind him. Arbat attacked him with a spear, aiming for his skull, but it struck his forehead and split his eyebrow, nose, eye, and lip, which is why he was called "the Split-Nosed" (al-Ashram). Then Atarah attacked Abraha from behind and killed him, and he took his place. The Najashi became angry, but he appeased him, and he was satisfied and confirmed him in his post.

Then he built in Sana'a a church the like of which had not been seen in its time, and he named it al-Qulays, with a damma on the qaf, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda, or it is said with a light lam, followed by a lower-dotted ya', then an unpointed sin, as in the Diwan al-Adab. He would bring to it marble of mixed colors and stones engraved with gold, as is said of the palace of Bilqis, the wife of Sulayman (peace be upon him). He wrote to the Najashi: "I have built for you, O King, a church the like of which has not been built before you, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs." When the Arabs spoke of this letter, a man from the Nassa'a, one of the Banu Fuqaym ibn Adi of Kinanah, became angry. He went out until he came to it and sat in it, that is, he relieved himself and smeared its qibla with his excrement. Then he left and returned to his land. Abraha was informed, and he said, "Who did this?" It was said: "A man from the people of this House to which the Arabs make pilgrimage in Mecca, who was angry when he heard your statement, 'I will divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs,' so he did this." Abraha was inflamed with rage and swore that he would march to the House until he demolished it.

It was also said: a group of Arabs lit a fire around it, and the wind carried it and burned it. So he was angered by this, and he ordered the Abyssinians, and they prepared and equipped themselves. He set out with sixty thousand men, so it is said, and with him was an elephant named Mahmud, which was strong and enormous, and twelve other elephants. It is also said eight, which is related from al-Dahhak. It is also said a thousand elephants. It is also said he had only Mahmud alone, and this is the view of most, and the most consistent with the apparent meaning of the verse. The Arabs heard of this, and they were greatly alarmed by it and became anxious about it, and they saw fighting him as a duty upon them. A man from the nobles and kings of Yemen, named Dhu Nafar, came out against him with whoever obeyed him from his people and from the rest of the Arabs. He fought him, was defeated, and was taken captive. Abraha wanted to kill him, but he said, "O King, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than killing me." So he let him go and kept him with him until, when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with those with him from his people and others. He fought him, was defeated, and was taken captive. He (Abraha) intended to kill him, but he said similar words to what preceded, so he released him, and he set out with him as a guide. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib ibn Malik al-Thaqafi came out to him with men from Thaqif, and said to him: "O King, we are only your slaves, who listen to you and obey you. There is no opposition to you from us. This house of ours, which you intend (they meant the house of al-Lat), is not what you seek; you seek the House in Mecca, and we will send with you someone to guide you to it." So he (Abraha) overlooked them. They sent with him Abu Righal, and he set out with Abu Righal until he brought him down at al-Mughammas, which is a known place on the road to al-Ta'if, pronounced like "mu'ammas" (with the ayn and the mim doubled). When he landed there, Abu Righal died and was buried there, and the Arabs stoned his grave, as Ibn Ishaq said.

It has been said: the grave there belongs to Abu Righal, a man of Thamud, who was Abu Thaqif, who had been in the Sanctuary (haram) and protected it. When he left it, he was struck by the punishment that befell his people at al-Mughammas, and he was buried there. This was preferred by the author of al-Qamus, citing a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan and others from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him). He said, before this, after quoting al-Jawhari: "It is not sound." Some reconciled by allowing that there are two graves for two men, each of whom is Abu Righal.

Then Abraha, while he was at al-Mughammas, sent a man from the Abyssinians called al-Aswad ibn Maqsur until he reached Mecca. He seized the wealth of the people of Tihamah from the Quraysh and others, and he captured two hundred camels, and it is also said four hundred camels, belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, who was then the chief of the Quraysh. The Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was in the Sanctuary intended to fight him, but they knew they had no power against him, so they held back. Abraha sent Hiyatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said: "Say to the chief of the people of this city: The King says, 'I have not come to fight you. I have only come to demolish this House. If you do not stand between it and war, I have no need for your blood. If he does not want to fight me, bring him to me.'" When Hiyatah entered, he was directed to Abd al-Muttalib. He told him what he had been ordered. Abd al-Muttalib said: "By Allah, we do not want to fight him, and we have no power to do so. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the House of His Friend Abraham (peace be upon him). If He protects it from him, it is His House and His Sanctuary. If He leaves between him and it, by Allah, we have no defense against him." Then Abd al-Muttalib set out with him, with some of his sons, until he reached the army. He asked about Dhu Nafar, who had been his friend. He entered upon him and said to him: "Do you have any help to give regarding what has befallen us?" He said: "What help can a captive man give, in the hands of a king who waits to kill him morning and evening? I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that I will send to Unays, the elephant-keeper, and I will entrust you to him, and I will magnify your right to him, and I will ask him to ask permission for you from the King, so that you may speak to him about what you wish, and he may intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do so." He (Abd al-Muttalib) said: "That is enough for me." So he sent to him, and he said to him: "Abd al-Muttalib is the chief of Quraysh and the lord of the spring of Mecca. He feeds the people in the plains and the wild animals on the mountaintops. The King has taken two hundred of his camels, so ask permission for him to see the King and benefit him with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do so."

So he spoke to Abraha and described Abd al-Muttalib as Dhu Nafar had described him, and he gave him permission. Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome and beautiful of people. When Abraha saw him, he honored him, so that he would not sit beneath him, and he disliked that the Abyssinians should see him seating him beside himself on his royal throne. So he came down from his throne, sat on his carpet, and seated Abd al-Muttalib with him on it beside him. The claim that he was overawed by him because of the light of prophethood that was on his face is weak, since it implies that the story happened before the birth of Abd Allah, and this contradicts what you know of the preferred view. Except that it could be said that the light manifested in him (in Abd al-Muttalib), even if it had already passed on [to Abd Allah]. Then he said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" He said: "My need is that the King return my camels to me."

Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you, since you have spoken to me about two hundred camels that I took for you, and you leave a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish. So do not speak to me about it."

Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "It could not be protected from me." He said: "You and that." In another narration, Thufanah ibn Adi, the chief of Banu Bakr, and Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah, the chief of Hudhayl, entered upon him with Abd al-Muttalib, and they offered him a third of the wealth of the people of Tihamah on condition that he return and not demolish the House, but he refused. He returned the camels to Abd al-Muttalib, and he departed to the Quraysh and informed them of the news. They took refuge on the peaks of the mountains, fearing the harm of the army. Then he (Abd al-Muttalib) stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and with him a group of the Quraysh, supplicating Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and seeking victory from Him. He said, while holding the ring:

O Allah, indeed a man defends his household,
so defend Your sanctuary.
And give victory against the family of the Cross
and its worshippers, this day, against Your family.
Let not their cross prevail,
nor their stratagem, as enemy, against Your stratagem.
They dragged the hosts of their lands
and the elephant, that they might take captive your dependents.
They aimed at Your sanctuary with their scheming,
out of ignorance, and they did not respect Your majesty.

The Most High's saying: ﴿Did He not make their plot into confusion?﴾ etc., is a general explanation of what Allah the Most High did to them. The hamza here is for taqrir (affirmative interrogation), as has already been explained. For this reason, what follows is joined by coordination to the interrogative clause, as if it were said: "Their plot has been made into the nullifying of the Ka'bah, its destruction and ruin, and the diversion of the nobility of its people to them, in waste and invalidation." Allah annihilated them with the most shameful annihilation. The root of tadlil (misguidance, here meaning frustration) is from "dalla 'anhu" when something is lost, and it is used here as a metaphor for invalidation. From this usage, Imru' al-Qays was called al-Dillil, because he lost his father's kingdom and squandered it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 105, verse 3:

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ i.e., groups (jama'at); it is the plural of ibbalah (إبّالَة), with a kasra on the hamzah and a shaddah on the unvowelled letter ba'. al-Farra' also reported ibalah (إبالَة) with a light pronunciation, and it means a large bundle of firewood. The group of birds was likened to it because of how they pressed together, and the word is also used for other things. From this is the verse of the poet:

"The camel was nearly broken by the noises, when the earth flowed with the swift, flocking ones (al-jurd al-ababil)."

It is said: its singular is ubul (أبُول), like ujul (عُجُول); it is said: ibbil (إبِّيل), like sikkin (سِكِّين); and it is said: abal (أبال). Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: it has no singular from its own form, like 'abadid (عَبادِيد); the firaq (فِرَق) of people are those who go off in every direction, and al-shamatit (الشَّماطِيط) are scattered pieces.

These birds came, as is narrated from a group, from the direction of the sea, and they were neither Najdi, nor Tihami, nor Hijazi. Some claimed that the pigeons of the Sacred Precinct (Haram) are descended from them; but this is not sound. Similar to this is what is reported from Hayat al-Hayawan (Life of Animals) that they build nests and hatch their young between the sky and the earth. The difference concerning their color has already been mentioned. And from 'Ikrimah: "It was as if their faces were like the faces of beasts of prey; they were not seen before that nor after it."

﴿Pelting them with stones﴾ is another descriptive clause for the birds. The present tense is used to narrate the scene and bring that striking image before the listener. Abu Hanifa, Abu Ya'mur (Abu Ya'mur), 'Isa and Talha, in one narration, read "yarmihim" (﴿يَرْمِيهِمْ﴾) with a yaʾ (the third-person masculine form). The hidden pronoun refers to the birds as well, and the masculine form is used because the birds are an ism jam' (collective noun, a noun that denotes a group but is singular in form). According to what al-Khafaji reported, the masculine is the required form for such nouns, and the feminine is used when they are taken to mean "a group" (al-jama'ah). It is also said that both forms are permissible, and this appears to be the apparent sense of Abu Hayyan's words. It is further said that the pronoun refers to your Lord, but this is not correct. The attribution of the aforementioned reading to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is reported by al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's work al-Bahr al-Muhit). However, the author of al-Nashr says that Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, has no reading at all, and that the readings attributed to him are fabricated.

﴿Of baked clay﴾ is a description of the stones, meaning: made of clay that has been turned to stone. It is an arabicised word (mu'arrab) from the Persian "sang-i gil" (سنك كل). It is also said that it is an Arabic word derived from al-sijl (السِّجْلِ), with a kasra, which means a large bucket. The meaning of the stones being from a bucket is that they came in a continuous, abundant flow, like water poured from a bucket. In this there is an implicit and imaginative metaphor (istiʿarah makniyyah wa takhyiliyyah).

It is also said that it is derived from al-ijsal (الإسْجال), meaning sending down, and the meaning is "from a thing that is sent down." In all of these explanations, "min" (from) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah). It is also said that it is derived from al-sijill (السِّجِلِّ), meaning a book, from which the word al-sijjin (السِّجِّينُ) was taken and made the name of the register in which the punishment of the disbelievers is recorded. The meaning then is "from among the punishment that is written and recorded," and "min" is partitive (tab'iyyah).

There is disagreement about the size of those birds, and likewise the size of those stones. It has been mentioned that the birds were like swallows (al-khataTIf), and that the stones were the size of chickpeas and lentils. Abu Nu'aym narrated from Nawfal ibn Abi Mu'awiyah al-Deyli that he said: "I saw the pebbles with which the companions of the elephant were pelted: they were pebbles the size of chickpeas and larger than lentils, red, with a seal, as if they were the stone of Zafar (jaz' Zafar)."

Abu Nu'aym, in al-Dala'il, narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Stones like pellets (al-bunduq)." In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from him: "Like the dung of sheep."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayd ibn Umayr that he said about the verse: "They are birds that came out of the direction of the sea, as if they were men of Sanda (rijal al-sanad), with stones like camels that kneel down, and the smallest of them like the heads of men. They did not aim at anyone among them without striking him, and they did not strike anyone without killing him." The reliable view is that the birds were the size of swallows, and that among the stones some were like a chickpea, and some smaller and some larger than that.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Abu Salih that there was written on the stone the name of the one it was thrown at and the name of his father, and that he saw this with Umm Hani.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 105, verse 5:

﴿So He made them like eaten straw﴾ — like the leaf of a crop upon which the devourer has fallen, that is, when worms have eaten it, or its grain has been consumed so that it remains empty of it. The speech on this interpretation involves an elision (hadhf) of a modifier (mudaf) with the modified noun (mudaf ilayhi) taking its place, or it is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). The comparison in this case is due to the departure of their souls while their bodies remained, or because the stones, by their heat, burned their insides. Others than one have held that the meaning is like chaff (tibn) eaten and excreted by animals, and what is meant is like dung (rawth), except that it was not mentioned with this word because of its vileness; it came in accordance with the courtesies of the Qur'an. Thus the severing of their joints is likened to the scattering of the parts of dung, and in this there is a display of the disfigurement of their state.

It is said: the meaning is like chaff that animals eat and excrete, and what is meant is that He made them in the position of chaff that animals are not prevented from, that is, degraded and wasted, none paying attention to them, nobody gathering them or burying them, like chaff in the desert upon which animals do as they wish for lack of any guardian over it. However, "ma'kul" (eaten) has been placed in the position of "akalat-hu al-dawabb" (the animals ate it), for the narration of the past in the form of the present; and it is as you see. And it seems that, since their coming was for the demolition of the Ka'bah, it was fitting that they be destroyed by stones; and since what provoked their anger was the fire of the Kinani (Udhrat al-Kinani), He, glory be to Him, likened them in what He did to them, according to the last opinion, to dung, or because what stirred it was its burning by what the wind carried of the fire of the Arabs, as you have heard, He, mighty and majestic, likened them in what He, exalted be His majesty, did to them to straw whose grain has been eaten, as we indicated to it last. Abu al-Darda' read, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh: "ma'kul" with a fatha on the hamza, following the vowel of the mim, and this is anomalous (shadhdh); and this is like their following in their saying "mahmum" with a fatha on the ha' for the vowel of the mim. And God Most High knows best.
